Speculative decoding accelerates inference by having a small draft model propose token sequences that a large target model then verifies or rejects in parallel; the implicit assumption is that the draft and target share enough of a probability landscape that draft proposals are accepted at a useful rate. The central question here is what happens to that acceptance dynamic when the two models have meaningfully different vocabularies or divergent distributions over a shared vocabulary — not just that throughput degrades, but that the pattern of rejections becomes systematically biased rather than random. An expert worries specifically about the distortion of the effective output distribution: naive implementations guarantee that the final sequence matches the target model's distribution in expectation, but that guarantee rests on rejection sampling math that assumes the draft's token probabilities can be meaningfully compared to the target's at each position — a comparison that breaks down subtly when vocabulary coverage differs, subword tokenization schemes diverge, or the draft was trained on a domain-shifted corpus that makes it overconfident in particular token clusters. The beginner sees acceptance rate as the single diagnostic number and optimizes it directly; the expert knows a high acceptance rate achieved by a draft that systematically steers proposals toward a biased subregion of the target's distribution is worse than a lower acceptance rate, because it corrupts outputs in ways that are statistically invisible without careful distributional auditing. Concretely, if a draft model underrepresents rare but semantically critical tokens — technical terms, low-frequency named entities, numerals in precise contexts — the rejection mechanism will prune those exactly when the target would have selected them, producing fluent but subtly wrong text at a rate that scales with task sensitivity.

The failure is insidious because high-frequency surface tokens — function words, common nouns, punctuation — tend to be stable across vocabularies and thus pass the ratio check cleanly, while the distortion concentrates in exactly the positions where meaning is load-bearing: precise numerical values, domain-specific terminology, morphological distinctions that a coarser BPE scheme collapses. The result is text that reads as grammatically and stylistically intact — because syntactic structure is carried by exactly the high-frequency tokens that sail through — while factual precision, entity identity, and numerical specificity degrade at a rate proportional to how far the draft's training distribution sits from the target's, which is neither visible in perplexity nor in standard fluency metrics.

Within a speculative window of length γ, accepted tokens before a rejection point become frozen context that the target's residual resample must condition on, creating a one-way ratchet: the resampled token is drawn from p_target(x_k | x_1...x_{k-1}) where x_1...x_{k-1} includes draft-accepted tokens that the target would not have generated had it been running autoregressively from the start. Across a window, this means each acceptance decision is made against a subtly corrupted prefix, and the corruption is strictly non-decreasing — Stern et al. and the SpecTr analysis both note that the distributional divergence between the speculative output and true target output grows with γ in the presence of draft-target mismatch, though the relationship is approximately linear in the well-matched case and becomes superlinear once the draft's systematic biases start compounding. The self-reinforcing threshold appears to emerge around γ = 5–8 tokens in practice, which is notable because this is exactly the window length that maximizes wallclock throughput in systems like DeepMind's implementation and vLLM's speculative decoding module — meaning the operationally optimal window sits at or just past the point where errors shift regime. The mechanism of self-reinforcement is semantic priming: once a frozen prefix has committed to a particular entity, numerical frame, or syntactic construction, the target's residual distribution at subsequent positions is itself narrowed toward completions consistent with that frame, so a draft-induced error in token 3 of a window makes draft-aligned (but target-misaligned) tokens more probable at positions 5–8, increasing their acceptance rate and making the distortion look like signal. What makes this particularly hard to detect is that the self-reinforcing regime produces higher acceptance rates than the linear regime, so the standard throughput diagnostic actually peaks at the point of maximum distributional corruption — an operator watching a dashboard would see the system performing best precisely when it is most compromised.

The most promising intervention sits in the verification step rather than the draft model: instead of accepting tokens greedily up to the first rejection, a speculative window rollback with distributional checkpointing periodically compares the joint probability of the entire accepted prefix under the target against what the target would assign to its own greedy continuation from the window's start, rejecting the whole window if the KL divergence exceeds a threshold — this breaks the ratchet by refusing to let early acceptances become frozen context when they've already steered the distribution. This approach was gestured at in the SpecTr paper and more concretely in Spector & Re's "Accelerating LLM Inference with Staged Speculative Decoding" (2023), where multi-stage verification with tree-structured proposals reduced distributional drift without proportionally reducing throughput, because most windows in practice don't trigger the rollback condition and the overhead is paid only when corruption would have been self-reinforcing. On the draft model side, the intervention that avoids retraining is vocabulary-aligned distillation: rather than using an off-the-shelf smaller model, systems like Medusa and EAGLE train draft heads directly on the target model's own residual stream, which by construction shares the target's vocabulary and internal probability geometry — EAGLE reported acceptance rates of 80–90% with genuine distributional fidelity because the draft is essentially a shallow extrapolation of the target rather than an independent model. The sampling procedure intervention that adds the least overhead is context-aware temperature scaling at resample positions: when the target resamples at a rejection point, applying a lower temperature forces the resample toward the target's mode rather than its full residual distribution, limiting how far the resampled token can deviate from what frozen prefix context implies — this doesn't eliminate the ratchet but prevents the resampled token from being an outlier that then primes subsequent draft overconfidence. The core tradeoff across all three interventions is that breaking the ratchet requires either more target model compute per window (rollback), constraining the draft architecture (EAGLE-style heads), or accepting mild output mode collapse (temperature scaling), and the throughput-fidelity Pareto frontier shifts depending on which regime dominates — for knowledge-intensive tasks the rollback approach recovers the most accuracy per FLOP spent, while for fluency-dominated tasks EAGLE-style heads offer the better tradeoff.

The smoothing bias manifests as a systematic underestimation of the target's confidence at high-certainty positions in rare contexts: when the target model encounters an unusual but highly constrained prompt — a precise mathematical proof step, a domain-specific code pattern, or a low-frequency idiomatic construction — it sharpens dramatically onto a near-deterministic token, but the EAGLE head, having averaged over a training corpus where that context was rare, produces a flatter distribution that spreads probability mass across plausible-but-wrong alternatives, causing unnecessary rejections at exactly the positions where speculative decoding should be most efficient. The inverse failure is more dangerous: in genuinely ambiguous OOD contexts where the target is itself uncertain and would distribute mass widely, the EAGLE head may have learned a spurious sharp prediction from superficially similar training examples, producing high-confidence draft proposals that the target rejects — but because the rejection triggers a resample from the target's broad residual distribution, the output is fine, while the throughput collapses precisely on the inputs that most need careful generation. The class of inputs where an independent draft model is strictly worse than EAGLE is well-understood: any input requiring deep vocabulary alignment, such as code completion mid-expression or multilingual text with script-switching. The class where EAGLE is strictly worse is narrower but more consequential: distributional extremes of the target's own training data, meaning inputs that activate rare but highly specialized target behaviors — few-shot prompts that trigger in-context learning regime shifts, adversarially structured inputs, or domain-specific formats like legal citations or chemical nomenclature where the target has sparse but sharply peaked knowledge. In these cases, an independent draft model trained specifically on that domain (a code-specialized 7B drafting for a general 70B target, for instance) can outperform EAGLE because its domain-specific training gives it genuine predictive accuracy in the tail, whereas the EAGLE head's smoothed representation of the target's residual stream has washed out exactly the sharp conditional structure that makes the target valuable there — this tradeoff was implicitly visible in EAGLE-2's ablations, where gains on coding benchmarks were smaller than on general text despite the architectural improvements, suggesting the head struggles most where token distributions are spikiest.

This entropy gating idea is implicit in the adaptive speculation length work from Google DeepMind's BatchSpec and more explicitly in "Online Speculative Decoding" (Liu et al., 2024), which used rolling acceptance rate as a proxy signal to adjust window length dynamically — but acceptance rate is a lagging indicator that averages over the window after the damage is done, whereas per-position entropy from the target is a leading indicator available before the window is committed. The practical obstacle is that dynamic strategy switching introduces scheduling overhead and complicates batching: in systems like vLLM where sequences are batched together, switching one sequence to a different draft strategy mid-generation requires either padding to accommodate heterogeneous window structures or maintaining separate draft model queues, and the engineering cost of this has prevented production deployment despite the theoretical clarity of the signal. The most actionable near-term implementation is a two-threshold system: entropy below 0.5 nats triggers single-token greedy target decoding (no draft at all, since acceptance is near-certain anyway), entropy between 0.5 and 2.0 nats uses EAGLE heads with standard window length, and entropy above 2.0 nats — genuine uncertainty — routes to an independent draft model or tree-structured proposals, recovering the throughput that EAGLE wastes by being overconfident in high-entropy contexts.

Entropy gating does not save wall-clock time in streaming settings — it redistributes compute identically to standard verification because the target forward pass that produces the entropy signal is the verification pass, meaning you've already paid the latency cost before you can act on the signal, and the only thing gating buys you is avoiding the subsequent draft forward passes and their verification, which matters for throughput across many tokens but contributes nothing to the latency of the token you're currently emitting. The genuine low-latency switching signal has to come from something that runs faster than the target model's forward pass, which points to three candidates: a lightweight probe trained on the target's intermediate layer activations, the draft model's own output entropy computed during its (cheaper) forward pass, or input-side features extracted before either model runs. The intermediate-layer probe approach is most promising and has concrete precedent: Schuster et al.'s "Confident Adaptive Language Modeling" (2022) showed that shallow classifiers trained on early transformer layer activations can predict final-layer output entropy with surprisingly high accuracy — if a similar probe trained on layers 8-12 of a 70B target can predict whether the final distribution will be sharp or diffuse, it runs in roughly 15-20% of the full forward pass latency and the prediction is available early enough to gate the draft strategy before committing the window. The draft model's own entropy is a weaker but zero-cost signal: if the EAGLE head is highly confident (entropy below 0.3 nats) and the last several tokens have had high acceptance rates, that correlates with the target also being in a sharp regime, providing a heuristic switch trigger that requires no additional compute — the failure mode is exactly the spurious overconfidence case described earlier, where EAGLE is sharp precisely when it shouldn't be trusted, so this signal has an adversarial correlation with the failure it's trying to detect. The most practically deployable low-latency signal is input-side: prompt segment classifiers trained to recognize domain, format, and structural features (code block delimiters, mathematical notation, citation patterns) that predict which generation regime the target will enter, running as a token-level tagger on the input before generation begins and setting per-segment draft strategy statically — this adds perhaps 2-5ms of prefill overhead and avoids all per-step switching cost, at the price of being unable to respond to distributional shifts that emerge mid-generation from the model's own outputs.
